utterances.text: And that 4D15 is simply the P2296, the main statement of the witness. What is it then?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 4D15 is another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've been told that's another document entirely. I don't even know if I've ever seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case it's unnecessary for us to deal further with it. Let's move ahead, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, it is. You can leave that one out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, I have introduced myself, so let's move only to the questions now. First of all, I would like to ask you something before the NATO bombing. Do you know that from the 23rd of February, 1999, until the 23rd of March, 1999, from the municipality of Kacanik 3.209 persons went to Macedonia? Are you aware of that? Do you know about the population from your area going to Macedonia even before the NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that, of the fact that the population was going to Macedonia before the NATO bombing began.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that in the area that you lived in, as far back as in February and the beginning of March there was pronounced activity on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't heard that there was KLA activity in this area. I mean, in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the neighbouring villages, that there was increased activity on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person named Loki Bashkim born in 1972 who lives -- or, rather, lived at the time in Kotlina, a member of the local police or, rather, the local guards?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this Bashkim Loku that I know who lived in Kotlina was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you do know of a person with that name, don't you?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know a person with that name, but I have no information about his activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that he and 12 others were kidnapped by the KLA and held in an improvised prison in Ivaja, and that that very person escaped on the 8th of March when the fighting in Ivaja started?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge about that, and I don't believe that that is true, because Bashkim lived in Kotlina, and I saw him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that on the 28th of February, 1990 -- 1999, Bogoljub Staletovic was killed, who was chief of police in Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that when the fighting began on the 8th and the 9th in Ivaja and your village was also encompassed by that fighting, did you know that 150 persons were taken into custody, and after that, 130 were subsequently released and the remaining 20 were held for further questioning?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to what happened in Ivaja on the 8th of March, this I don't know. I wasn't there. I may only talk to you about what happened in Kotline. And this thing, I don't know what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The distance between Ivaja and your village is about 1.500 metres; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is four to five kilometres away. It is true, however, that on the 8th of March in Kotline we heard shots, but we didn't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you something about the young men for whom you said the -- joined the KLA. And you said that they joined the KLA somewhere in the mountains. Do you have in mind the mountains in the immediate vicinity of your village?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that the youths became members of the KLA. I am talking about my own village. I told you there were -- there were no members of the KLA from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall back to it -- come back to it still at a later point. As regards the two pits for which you claimed were supposed to be wells, is it customary to dig two holes when looking for a well, which are so close to each other in order to try and find water?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you will be trying our patience, I think, if we're back in the territory of the wells. We have to get an overall perspective on this case, and when one counsel has explored a matter in some detail, it really -- it can't be necessary, I think, to go over it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our position is those holes actually have been dug during the war, or immediately before the war, that those were not well holes, but I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why don't you just put that simple question. I mean, you know, the question didn't give me any inclination that that's what you were actually going to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the witness said that he had never saw those holes before, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. No, Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to use his common knowledge and his -- him being living on the village. But I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, today in the transcript, on page 7, you were quoted what you stated in the Milosevic trial. "[In English] [Previous translation continues] ... in our village, and whoever wished to join KLA ranks, he might do so because KLA troops were in the mountains." [Interpretation] That is why I asked you whether any of the young men of your village joined the KLA in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave you the answer earlier, and I'm clear about the question, and I said this before this trial -- before the Milosevic trial in this Tribunal. I meant that those who wished to join the KLA knew where to find it, and they went there. And I may tell you also that from my village there were KLA members, soldiers, who operated in other parts of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't know what was taking place beyond the borders of your village, may we conclude that you don't know what the reason for military action was since you were not familiar with the -- any actions undertaken by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think, Mr. Lukic, the witness is claiming to have knowledge about the purpose of military action, and it's not a question that's going to assist us in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will go briefly, Mr. Loku, to the spelling, and my learned friend Mr. Ackerman asked you about this. I wanted to ask you the following: Is it correct that in the Albanian language a hole or a pit is spelled in both the singular and the plural -- oh, actually, I wanted to ask you only about the singular, g-r-o-p-a. In the plural, it is g-r-o-p-e. Am I correct, or have I been misinformed?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are not informed. "Grope" is singular. "Gropa" is plural.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So I put it the other way around. But fact is that the singular and the plural are not spelled out the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just check the record just in case it may be important. The answer at 52:15, that's the last answer, 52:14 -- oh, it has been corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you saw those people who, according to you, were being taken towards the pits, were they tied up in any way?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were holding their hands above their heads. I couldn't see if they were tied up in any way. I only could see their hands above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, yesterday, in the updated version, on page 69, line 24, this was entered: "[In English] The people who had their hands tied were taken there." [Interpretation] I just wanted to double-check with you. Therefore, this portion of the transcript is incorrect, that their hands were tied.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the transcript is not correct. I meant to say that the way I saw them holding their hands above their heads you might take it to be tied. I couldn't say, you know. But it seemed to me that they were holding their hands -- or I saw them holding their hands above their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Although you didn't approach the pits, did you know whether they were used for any purpose?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: These pits were not used for any purpose. I told you. These are not the only pits that exist in the village, because as I said to you, people dig holes or pits for water, because our villagers dig many holes before they can find water. If they happened to dig one and two and don't find any water, then they give it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, 1999, apart from some other pits, were there -- apart from -- interpreter's correction. On the 24th of March, 1999, were there any other bodies found by any other pits?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, that was the day that the bodies were found on the two pits, but not on any other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what time it was when all this was taking place, as you put it, when those people were being taken to the pits?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: When those people were being taken to the pits was 1.00 or 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement in the English page 5, last paragraph, and the sixth page, first paragraph; in the Albanian, page 6, paragraph 4, you state that all this was taking place at around 3.30 in the afternoon. Which of the two is correct?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that it occur in the afternoon. From the place they were taken, from the clinic to the pits, it took them over an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How far is the clinic from the pits?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the crow flies not more than 150 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What can we conclude, therefore? Were these people by those pits at 3.30 or between 1.00 and 2.00?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I mean, the last thing on earth people do in situations that we're dealing with here, whether in military conflict or otherwise, unexpected events happen, you don't -- when unexpected -- you don't keep your eye on the clock so that seven years later you can tell people the exact time at which it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I have a reason for this, Your Honour. I'll try to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I read your statement only, I didn't have this time designation at that time. In your statement dated the 4th of June, 1999, in the English page 3, paragraph 4; in the Albanian page 4, paragraph 4; and in the B/C/S, page 3, paragraph 3, you speak of the 9th of March, which is two weeks prior to the event, and you state: "It was almost dark by the time. My guess is that it was around 3.30 p.m." What sort of visibility did you have at that time of day as you observed the events unfold?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you've mixed up two days. The 4th of March refers to something else, the 24th of March to something else. The 24th of March refers to the incident at the pits. The 9th of March refer -- refers to the first offensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Loku. I believe I stressed that, and I also said that two weeks elapsed between the two events. And I don't think one could enjoy much more daylight between the 9th and the 21st of March. Therefore, as you were observing all this, what sort of visibility did you have? Was it dark? Was it closer to midday? Could you please explain this to me?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was before dusk. Usually it became dark at 4.35 [as interpreted]. It depended on the weather, because in March it still snows with us. It depends on the weather, as I said. There is fog. There is snow. Night comes earlier. If it's a bright day, it is brighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell how much time passed from the moment when, according to you, the people were being thrown into the pits?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Clarification for the transcript. I have at line 55 -- 15, it being written that it usually became dark at 4.35, when I thought I heard it was 4.30 or 5.00. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Loku, that it was before dusk. Usually it became dark at. Now, what time did you give?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After 4.00 I said. I didn't look at my clock, but it is known when dusk comes or when night comes with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's the penalty of asking questions, Mr. Stamp. I heard 4.35, I may say, but I'm not -- but when I think about it it's an odd answer as well, but anyway, let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was trying to ask you something, and I believe I'll have to repeat the question. From the moment when -- when according to you these people were being thrown into the pits and the moment when you heard the explosion, how much time did elapse?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the bodies were thrown into the pits and after the explosion I heard, it took some half an hour between the two events. So the explosion was heard after half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. During that half an hour, as you said on page 4, line 12, you didn't see anyone except the soldiers and the police as you stated. Therefore, according to you, there were no Serb civilians. Did you see a woman in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see people taking photographs on the spot?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Today you were shown some photographs on which one can see holes and dead bodies next to the holes. You told us that in your village of Kotlina you didn't find any dead bodies by some other pits or holes. It is our defence's position, Mr. Loku, and there is also official documentation to corroborate it, that on that day, on the very spot there was an official commission headed by an investigative judge. The judge was a lady in civilian clothes. They carried out an on-site investigation after the fighting that took place in which some KLA soldiers were killed. It is our position that what you are stating is correct, that you indeed were watching the event or, rather, had you been watching the event you should have seen the investigation team before the explosion, since it is clear that in the photographs we can see open holes which haven't been covered with dirt. Do you still maintain --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm trying not to object, but we have gone on for more than a half a page of transcript of assertions of the Defence position without the witness being asked a specific question about each assertion so he could address each one. I think really what the line of questioning is did he see something or did he see something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's already said that he didn't see any on-site investigation. What is the question, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, is it still your position that you observed the event from the moment when the people were brought to the pit, throughout the execution, as you called it, and then it being thrown into the pit as well as the process of covering those pits or closing them by using explosives?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We observed it during the entire time. We observed everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You say at that there were no KLA members in your village.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have repeat it had several times. It is true that there weren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm slightly distracted. Judge Chowhan would like you to tell us whether these -- what we see in the picture are caves rather than holes. What is your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they are not caves. They are holes. And I know the person who have dug up those holes in order to find water in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Lukic, can you -- explain to me what is the point you're making about the investigating judge. Are you saying the investigating team was there before the explosion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's obvious they've photographed the holes with ladders inside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then weren't there when the explosion took place. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Our claim is that it's not done by Serb forces for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. But you're saying an investigating team had been there before there was an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes, Your Honour. They investigated and found some dead bodies outside the wells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this what you infer from the circumstances, or have you got eyewitness evidence to tell you that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have official documentation. We haven't spoken with anybody regarding this specific issue, but we have the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's one of these circumstances, I imagine, where the official documentation may not be entirely helpful for us having heard what is purported to be eyewitness testimony. Anyway, is there anything else you need to explore with the witness or have we exhausted the topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This topic I did, but I have a few more. Not too long, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We've dealt with that, that is that you said that there was no KLA presence in your village, but after the fighting in Ivaja, obviously the KLA was retreating. Do you know in what direction the KLA was retreating from Ivaja?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the direction the KLA was retreating from Ivaja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your village there are three hamlets, Mahala Dreshec, Donja Reka and Reka e Poshtme and Gornja Reka or Reka e Eperme. Was a single house destroyed in the hamlets of Donja Reka and Gornja Reka?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the neighbourhoods of Reka e Poshtme there were no burnt houses but there were burnt houses in other neighbourhoods as well as in the centre of the village where the entire population was after the 24th of March. The other neighbourhoods were empty because, as I said, the villagers were all gathered in the centre of the village where the school was, where the mosque was. The other neighbourhoods were empty. The people were in the biggest Mahala, or neighbourhood, which is in the centre of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Isuf Loku, father's name Nazmi from Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In his statement that he gave to the OTP of this Tribunal in the English version it's page 2, the last paragraph, and in the first paragraph of the third page he claims that not a single house in the other two neighbourhoods was destroyed in your village. Do you still stand by your statement that some houses were destroyed in addition to Mahala Dreshec, I mean outside Mahala Dreshec?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We're referring to a document here. I wonder if that was furnished to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I was wondering if that was delivered to us in accordance with the order of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I would expect you to mention them before you actually try to use it. I don't think it's courtesy to the Court just to try to slip it through that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement, on page 3, paragraph 1, B/C/S; English version page 3, paragraph 2; and Albanian version, page 3, paragraph 2, you say: "Members of the Yugoslav army and police started shooting at the convoy in order to warn them not to move on further." How many persons in the convoy were killed after this shooting?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said refers to 9th of March. This convoy had approached Dreshec neighbourhood, and Isuf Loku that you mentioned earlier is from this neighbourhood. Every house in this neighbourhood was burned. The population was fired at, but there were no victims on that day. The population was only prevented to go towards Gllobocica, towards the border, and they had to return to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, can we conclude, then, that there was no shooting, that is to say, no firing at the column or convoy?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was in firing at the Serb forces on the 9th of March or on the 24th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Maybe I wasn't precise. Maybe I should repeat the question. Is it correct that in actual fact no one fired at the column or convoy? Had that kind of gunfire been opened at the convoy, somebody would have had to get killed.

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gunfire wasn't opened at the people but in their vicinity, and they were prevented from proceeding with their journey towards the border. There were no persons that were killed on that day, but there were no provocations either from their side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's how the English has been translated, "in the general direction."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Mr. Loku. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic -- sorry. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. [In English] I have some questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Loku. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence counsel in the Defence team of General Vladimir Lazarevic. As for the village of Kotlina that you're from, is it also subdivided into Gornja Kotlina and Donja Kotlina, as in upper and lower Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My village is called Kotlina, but there are neighbourhoods in the village. You have the Dreshec neighbourhood, the neighbourhood of Reka e Eperme, of Reka e Poshtme. These three neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And is there this subdivision into Gornja and Donja Kotlina, lower and upper Kotlina?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There isn't such a subdivision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that your brother, Milaim, was killed before the 24th of March, 1999. Could you tell us whether he was a teacher by profession?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did he work in the school where you were principal?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Was your member -- your brother Milaim a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother Milaim was not a member of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a statement which is in the system, and I would like 5D7 to be shown. This is a statement made by an Albanian given to the employees of the MUP of Serbia, that is to say the investigation authorities, and it's on the electronic disclosure system U004-1963.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It is with regret that I rise during the cross-examination on points like this, but we really ought to be notified about these documents. Perhaps we were and it's just slipped through, but could counsel indicate whether or not we were notified, as instructed, about these documents?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, as you know, we sent it yesterday to the system, but I also have enough hard copies with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, no. You are to give a list. Immediately the witness is sworn you have to give a list to the Prosecutor of the documents you may be relying upon. Whether they're in the system or not, that's a separate requirement. Now, have you done that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Your Honour, as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You gave him a list saying, "We will rely upon these documents in --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just received the information that we didn't send by e-mail to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, move on to something else, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But we put that in electronic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. Move on. You've got to comply with the rules here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Could we please have 3D86 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Hebib Thaqi statement, born in 1965, given to the investigators of the OTP on the 29th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the question? What's the question, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that witness said that he was a member of the KLA, and he speaks of what happened on that day in the village of Kotlina. The person who gave this statement says that for himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is your question to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the KLA was present in the village itself on that day, the 24th, when the fighting took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I will not allow you to ask that question which has been answered repeatedly. Now, what is the question you now want to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know Mr. Hebib Thaqi?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know a person by that name. There is no one with the last name Thaqi in Kotline. Loku, Kuci, these are the last names you can find in Kotlina. And if you ask me for people with these last names, I can answer you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness a part of this statement, which is on page 3, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just ask him a question. What is the question you want to ask him? Why do you need the statement? I'm trying to help you to get on with your --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Four times I've asked you to ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I understood completely. I just tried to challenge some allegations from -- from the statement with comparation with that statement. That was my intention, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, ask him the question first of all, because he might agree with what you're going to say without you putting a statement to him. It's only when you've got something that he may disagree with that a statement could ever arise. And it's even doubtful if you should be using someone else's statement to challenge him anyway. You may say that you've information, what's your position on this information? You don't need to tell him unless he asks you, or unless the Prosecutor insists that you have a foundation that's disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I understood, Your Honour. I do apologise if I disturbed this Honourable Trial Chamber, but ... May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loku, are you aware of the fact that on the 23rd of March, 1999, in the territory of the entire Federal Republic of Yugoslavia a state of imminent threat of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 9th to the 24th of March, we were in darkness in our village. We didn't know what was going on in our own village, let alone the entire territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you know that an invention by NATO was being prepared?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't know what was being prepared by NATO, but on the 25th of March when I went to Macedonia, I heard from other citizens that NATO had intervened in Kosova, and I was happy to hear that because that made -- that meant that other people who had remained in Kosova would be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that it's a bit illogical that when the NATO interventions start by way of bombing we have movement by tanks, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Argumentative. It's not for him to work out for you the logics of this. He's here to give evidence of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Loku, did you support the KLA in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I won't allow you to ask that question again. It's been repeatedly asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I haven't got any further question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And next time we will carry on about electronic disclosure system and e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Do you have re-examination, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Just one or two questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown your OSCE statement and a passage was cited from it. Not your statement, but the record of an interview in which you said -- or it was read to you that the group from the ambulance building was forced to walk to a well near the ambulance building, and later on in cross-examination you said you not only marked the ambulance building on a map, but you said that from the clinic to the holes was about 150 metres. When you say "the clinic," is that the same as the ambulance building?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear from your examination-in-chief. It's clear from the cross-examination. I don't think that question needs to be answered either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That being clear, Mr. Loku, can I take it, then, that your evidence or your evidence here today is substantially consistent with the record from the OSCE interview report in which you say that the men were taken from the ambulance building towards the hole where they were killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I expect six objections to that question. That's not for the witness to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said that the record of interview to the OSCE is incorrect to the extent that it is incomplete. Now, what I want to ask you is this: Is it correctly recorded here as read to you that you told them that the men were taken from the ambulance building to the hole where they were thrown? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object, because that's not what the report says. It doesn't say anything about a hole. It talks about a well. So if he's going to ask him about what it says, he ought to at least, you know, quote it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've had enough of this, Mr. Stamp. If you've another subject to deal with, move on to that, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said, and I'm trying to find the quote, but since I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll take our break now if that's going to help you find it, but I thought we might have got to the next witness by now. However, we'll be back at 6.00 in the hope that we can make rapid progress.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, before he proceeds, may I bring to your attention what may or may not be a serious problem in the transcript? I hate to do this, but it could be serious. If you go, like, half way up to where we would get to page 36 and we take a recess at 3.49 p.m., it then -- and I'm supposed to be coming back and cross-examining at that point. Instead it throws in apparently the beginning of the cross-examination of Mr. Visnjic from earlier in the day and starts over at paragraph 1 at page 1. And then it goes down through page 2 and starts over at page 1 again where it picks up my cross-examination at page 2, line 21, and apparently leaves out some of the cross-examination that I had begun at that point. In other words, there's just -- it looks like a part of my cross has been replaced by a part of Mr. Visnjic's cross, which probably isn't a bad thing because he may have been doing a better job than I was anyhow. In any event, it looks like some of mine is missing and I don't know how that's fixable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Well, that's for those dealing with the transcripts to resolve, and we'll get a report from them on how it is resolved. Nothing we can do at this minute on it, but thank you for alerting us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me just make sure my concern is understood. If we let the witness go and find out that that part of cross-examination was completely lost, I don't think we can get it back without having the witness here. That's my concern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that will depend on the recording of the evidence as well, which is a separate matter. It would also depend on the notes I've been taking as we go along because they may be good enough without -- because I take my own notes as we go. I don't rely on the electronic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. And we do have a recording that we could replay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But we'll get a report and deal with it expeditiously. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Loku, you said that there was a council that organised reburial of persons in the cemetery in Kacanik. What council were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a council on the reburial of the victims, because there was a ceremony organised to bury the victims, and people came there to express condolences to our village. People from all over came to the place to attend the burial ceremony. So this is the council I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You said that they were buried there because it contributed to the national cause. You also said that they may have been buried there if they were killed in fighting. But you also said that if you had been killed that you don't know where you would have been buried. Can I ask you to clarify that? Do you know of the criteria that was used by these persons to determine who would be reburied in the cemetery at Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: HAZBI LOKU [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the criteria they used because I was not a member of the council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I have nothing further. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 4D13 and 14 we will mark for identification pending submission by Mr. Ackerman of the marked extracts from the transcript that he seeks to have admitted, and allowing a period, a very brief period for others to comment if they have any remarks to make on the question whether they should be admitted or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it's of any help, we would not at this stage object to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that. But I think it was very sensible to try to identify the bits that really matter and not to have the whole transcript produced to no good end. I'm sorry it gives you a little extra work, Mr. Ackerman, but I understood the work was largely done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the work is completely done. It's here. I know every page that I would like to have referred to, and I could either put it in the record now or I could extract those pages and make them a separate exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. If you can just read them off just now that would save everybody and another rain forest. Pages 1928 through 1932. 1936, 1937.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you said through 1932, not 1931. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: 28 through 31. 1928 through 1931 [sic]. 1936 through 38. 1940 and 41 and 42. 2002, 2004, 2005, 2015, 2018, 2026. I'm just checking to make sure the transcript is correct. And it's 4D12 and 13, Your Honour, that the full transcripts are in. And that's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The problem arises now that some of them were not referred to with the witness, and even in respect to at least one of them that was referred to, I had considered re-examination using the transcript to put that aspect of it in better context, and then I thought it would be better to adopt the suggestion that the transcript goes in and not having to go through all of these. Now, some of these references may well be along a legitimate line that the Defence might want to take, but if we explore them we might find that we would also want the Court to consider other relevant bits of the evidence to have everything in context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, say that again. If we explore them --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Some of these references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. I have no objection to that. I said we would allow you a limited time to make submissions on it, if you wish, so that you can have other pieces added. So we'll allow 48 hours for you to make a submission if you wish other parts of the transcript added.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But rather than have the whole thing without having any real focus at all. So we'll allow you until the end of the week, on Friday afternoon, to make any submission to us that you wish. You can do it either orally or in writing. And if any other counsel feels the need, then he or she should do so, but bearing the mind the concern we have to be as economical as possible. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: No, I don't have actually some things which is connected with this witness, but I just -- [Interpretation] I just wanted to ask you for your leave to provide you with further clarifications once the witness has left the courtroom. This concerns some documents unrelated to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well, Mr. Loku, that completes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the first clarification concerns 3D74 being the report, the forensic report concerning the location. What I wanted to mention is an explanation as to why the photographs we used are of such poor quality, namely we asked the National Council for Documentation relating to the municipality of Kacanik. Among the documents we received, there is a file missing pertaining to Kotlina. What we received instead is a note in which one can read that the entire file was put at the disposal of the National Council. On the other hand, in the OTP database this document is in black and white, and at the same time it was used by Milosevic Defence. It was put through two of his witnesses. What I showed you today is an MFI copy from the Milosevic case. That is why this copy is black and white. What we will try to do on our part is to try to get coloured copies which would probably clarify what we were trying to see. As regards 3D72, this is a photograph of the KLA cemetery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on to that, I don't think the witness was -- was handicapped in any way by the quality of the photographs in 3D74, but I take the point you make about the quality. I mean, he did say with --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. We may have had some additional questions for the witness. It wasn't to his detriment in any case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next exhibit is 3D72, being a photograph of the cemetery on the Kacanik-Urosevac road. As you were able to see, the photographs were taken from a distance, from outside the cemetery. What I was able to do was to take photographs of only a part of the tombstones, and this happened quite accidentally because the column we were part of on the 23rd -- on the 24th of May stopped there to take a short rest, this being the crossroads which we were meant to take. We were not allowed to enter the cemetery, and we were not allowed to enter another place where we also wanted to take some photographs from up close. As regards the names of Loku and the rest, we came across those by chance, because once we took the photographs, we were able to realise that some of the names are also mentioned in the indictment as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you should make it clear who didn't allow you to enter the cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, concerning the delegation, there was an interpreter. He introduced himself -- or she introduced herself as an interpreter, and she -- or he explained the main person in charge of security that it would be inappropriate for us to enter the premises. And this happened on two occasions on that trip. The entire business of taking photographs happened by chance. Apart from the people there, there was someone from The Hague Tribunal. I believe someone from the OTP being part of the column. And this piece of information that we were at the cemetery and that we took photographs is nothing secret. It wasn't a covert operation or nothing that could be implied as such. As regards 3D88, these are photographs of the village of Kotlina.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were taken on the 24th of May in the afternoon around 2.00 p.m. We were in this village where the two pits are, and this is the only explanation I can provide at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These are the sort of documents that when you come to present your own case you will hopefully be considering as candidates for presentation through written evidence or by stipulation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. I agree, Your Honour. I wanted to make use of this witness to try and confirm some locations, because once in the field one is often uncertain what is what, and I'm quite happy to have received some answers from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, for not the next witness but the one after that there's an application for the evidence to be taken in closed session, and that application is obviously late and requires dispensation of -- from compliance with -- with the rules. Is this something you're familiar with, or is it Mr. Hannis who is dealing with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis -- Mr. Hannis will be more familiar with it, but I might be able to address any concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. O'Sullivan, obviously if this witness is potentially going to start giving evidence tomorrow, or even on Thursday, we have to decide to deal with the application and deal with it, or if there are good reasons to refuse to deal with it. Is there a common Defence position in relation to this application?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I think there can be by first thing tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's one of these situations where between you you may know more about the situation -- more about the circumstances of the witness than -- than we need to know and can come -- can come to an arrangement. If you can't, then obviously we will have to hear submissions about it if there's a willingness at least to have the matter dealt with with a view to hearing the evidence in the course of this week. So we'll deal with that matter first thing tomorrow morning, if that's convenient. Sorry, tomorrow afternoon. First thing tomorrow afternoon. And meanwhile we shall start the evidence of the next witness. Who is?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Sejdi Lami.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Wait a minute, sorry. We have another comment. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make a very brief observation. I'm not sure that I have a solution to it. With many of these witnesses we're using their witness statements, like in this one, P2296 is coming in basically as a substitute in many cases for their live testimony which, you know, obviously saves us time and is a good thing in many cases. But the thing that I began to become concerned about today was on I think every occasion where I referred the witness to this statement as is to what he'd said in the statement he said no, I didn't say that, or that's a bad translation or something like that. And then one begins to wonder to what extent we really can rely on what's contained in these statements, because I know that both the Prosecution, the Defence and the Chamber will tend in the future to rely on everything that in here that wasn't talked about as being basically the testimony of the witness under oath. And I'm just starting to worry about the credibility of it all. And I don't have a suggestion or a solution. I've just become concerned about it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, it's something on which we will reflect, particularly the point that you mention about the alleged mistranslation, and we will try to give some guidance on this as soon as possible. Now, Mr. Stamp. The witness is Sejdi Lami; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lami, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And this is a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Indeed, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can you tell me the paragraphs of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is paragraph 72(k)(3), 75(k)(2), and Schedule K.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lami.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Now, Mr. Lami, we already have in writing information you have given to the Office of the Prosecutor. The purpose of this afternoon's hearing and tomorrow, you will continue to give evidence tomorrow, is to enable the counsel representing the parties here, that's the Prosecution and the accused, to ask you questions either to add to the information you've already given, to clarify it, or to challenge it. But asking I'd ask you to have particularly in mind, it doesn't help us to hear again the same information as we already have before us. It's important for us to get as much Information, especially new information, as we can. So it would be a great help to everyone, including yourself, if you will listen very carefully to every question and confine your answer to the particular point that the question relates to. The first person to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution, and that is Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you please state your name and spell your surname as well.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: My last name is spelled L-a-m-e [as interpreted], and first name is Sejdi, S-e-j-d-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. We have your last name spelled here as L-a-m-e. That is not correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's certainly correct on the transcript, I think. L-a-m-i.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I see, Mr. Lami, that there may well be a clarification that you want to make in respect to the spelling of your last name.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: It's not a problem at all. In all my documents, it's L-a-m-a, Sejda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And -- but you spelled it as L-a-m-i. What is correct and how do you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I am called Lami Sejdi, but in my documents it's Lama Sejda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Do you recall -- before I get to that, where do you live, sir? From where are you from? Where are you from?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: In the municipality of Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in which village in Kacanik?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: The village of Vata.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you give a statement to a member of the OTP on the -- in July 2000, in respect of events that occurred there in 1999?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And you came here to testify, that is you came to The Hague to testify about those events in January 2002, and on that occasion you -- you declared -- you gave a declaration that the statement was true and correct before a certifying officer. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That 92 bis statement and the package, complete package, for the record, is P02271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In your statement at page 4 in the English version, and since you don't have it I'll just read the relevant part to you, and I'm referring to the second full paragraph of page 4 in the English version, you say that one Avdi Bajgora went to the village and he had a meeting with a man from the village who was a member of the SPM [sic] party and his name was Murtezan Lami. That is what is in the statement. Is there any clarification you would like to make in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: May I speak now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: He was not a representative of the Serbs this Murtezan Lami, but he was a poor man, the person that Avdi Bajgora visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "was not a representative of the Serbs," do you mean that he was not a member or was he a member of the SPS party, the person that Avdi Bajgora met?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: He was not a member because he couldn't be a member of either Albanian or Serbian party. He was a poor man. He had nine children. He had no interest whatsoever to become a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 2 of your statement in the English version which I'll read to you again because you don't have the translation, and I'm referring to the last paragraph of that page, Your Honours, you said that one week before the Serb attack on the village on the 13th of April, 1999, some 20 KLA soldiers came and established themselves in a house. They started digging some trenches there. Can I ask you, how far was this house that the KLA soldiers went to from your house? And you can approximate.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: May I speak now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: About 2 to 300 metres. This house was far from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did these KLA persons who went to that house, 20 of them you said, were they in uniform or were they not in uniform or partly so?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Half of them in uniforms and the other half in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where did they start the excavation of this trench? Can you say where that was in relation to the village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: In -- it's above my house in Lama neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: About how far from the village were they digging this trench?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: About 200 metres above my house, in a hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I take you now to paragraph 4 of page 4 of the English version of your statement, and here you speak of a killing of four persons, and you said in that statement: "I was hiding in a gorge by the stream together with my family. From there I could not observe the soldiers. Later I heard that the soldiers captured four men from the village. The men were brought up and down to the village four times and on the fourth trip they were killed. My wife told me that she heard the four men -- my wife told me that she heard the men screaming before they were killed."

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you tell us firstly exactly what it is your wife told you she observed?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: My wife said to me, because I was in this stream about 10, 15 metres below while my wife was in a meadow where there were about 150 people, children, elderly persons. So she said to me they captured these four men. They walked them up and down the village three, four times, and wounded them and ultimately killed them and that she heard them screaming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did she tell you whether or not she saw anything?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No. She saw them because they were on a hill about 300 metres up, and she -- she saw that. As the crow flies is the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: How far was she away from you at the time?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: At that time, my wife was, as the crow flies, 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From? How far was she from you?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: From me she was 10, 15 metres far because I was in a stream below there, and they couldn't see me and I couldn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. If you can, can you just tell us what it is she said that she saw?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: My wife saw them when they were captured while they were still alive, how they were walked and how they were killed. She could see that because this was on a hill up. You could see from there. And when we went there after three hours, after they withdrew, we found three dead bodies and another one which was about 20 metres away from the other three. He was stabbed and his intestines were out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did she say how they were killed and by whom?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: She didn't know who killed them because you cannot recognise the face of a person who killed them from 300 metres but you could see that it was army. They had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can I take you finally to page 5, paragraph 3 of your statement, the English version, and I'll read it to you again and ask you about it. You said in addition to the four persons that you spoke of earlier in your statement: "Later that day or the same day there were brought seven more bodies to the village. They were killed in the surrounding neighbourhoods of Kaka and Tifeku. But since the cemetery is here, they were brought to the same house as the others." Can you remember the names of any of the other seven who were brought to your village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I remember some of the names but not all of them. Those that were close to my house I remember them, and those that were further from my house I don't know their names. I don't remember them now at this moment. I know the name, the father's name, of those brothers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. What are the names of those that you know of the seven that were brought later?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: The first that was brought was the son of Osman Caka. His name is Ilir. Fifteen years old he was. The second is Jakup Caka, a cousin of the first. The third is Shyqyri. He's from Gacica but he's an in-law of the above two who were sheltering there with the Caka family. Then Ramadan Xhokli who was also sheltering with the Caka family. I don't know if he is a member or not, but personally I've seen him in civilian clothes. And Rahim Lami, and I'm a witness to him. Hebib Lami, Brahim Lami, Jakup Caka. Rahim Lami had his two eyes gouged out by those who perpetrated his killing. Hebib Lami had the sign of cross made on his chest. Brahim Lami was killed on his forehead, and Jakup had about seven or eight bullets in his body and he was stabbed. There are others as well, but I don't know their names. I've only stated in my statement about these four persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch the four names that the witness mentioned in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, they're in the statement, I think. The witness actually gave seven names there, I think, having said that he couldn't remember all the names. Are we sure that we're hearing the names of the seven bodies brought to the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I just clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Slowly if you can, sir, can you just name those persons among the seven that were brought to the village, if you remember their names, and do so slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: The first is Ilir Osman Caka, Osman being father's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have no doubt we've got seven names. I don't need to hear them again. I just wanted to be sure that we're talking about same thing in view of the introduction that he couldn't remember all the names. And then we -- we've got a reference to 11 bodies later. Are they different? Are you going to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I probably should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. If you go on to that that will make it clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You mentioned the names in your statement of Mahmut Caka, Hebib Lami, Rahim Lami, and Brahim Lami. These were the persons that your wife observed being killed and whose bodies you later found in the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All is clear now. Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the other three bodies you mentioned were those that were later brought from the neighbouring areas of the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He mentioned seven others. He's given you seven in addition to the first four.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've got Ilir Caka. In fact, I can't read my transcript when I go back when it's at the end of the page. It then gives you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilir. It's with an R in the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's been transcribed wrongly. It then gives you a second one, who is a cousin of his. He then gives you the third one, who is from Gacica. Then there was -- I mean, there are seven names there. So we now have 11 names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Four names --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there are 11, but I don't know the names of all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see. Well, I don't know why I can't get to the end of my transcript so I can't read what I've got in front of me, but I'm convinced there are seven names there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, there are, but the latter four names he went on to mention those but those are the same four that he has just said were the ones his wife observed being killed that he saw in the village. I was asking about another seven persons who were later brought to his village, and of those seven he could only remember three of their names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where the others were wounded. I do know some of their names but I don't know all of them. I can tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's my mistake. I follow that now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lami. There may be some other questions required of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. General Pavkovic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, General Lukic, General Lazarevic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Lami, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this case. I have very few questions to ask you, and I think with the exception the first one that you can answer them very easily by either saying either yes or no, and if you do that we'll be finished in just a very short time. In your statement at paragraph 9, you talk about the KLA in your village and the activities they were carrying on there, and you say that on the 12th of April, the day before the attack on your village, they were ordered to get out of the village. Can you tell us who ordered them to get out of the village?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I have no information why they went away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So is it that you don't know they were even ordered? You don't know about an order?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: I couldn't go there and talk with them because my house where they were staying was 300 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the answer is you don't know and that's all I'm asking. There were 11 persons killed in or in the vicinity of your village and you didn't see the killing of any of those persons, did you? You can just say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the only thing you know about the identity of people who killed some of these people was what your wife had told you. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: She told me about four people, and I know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that the people who committed these offences were wearing camouflage uniforms and that they were army. The only reason you identify them as army is because they were wearing camouflage uniforms. You didn't actually determine that they were actual serving members of the army of Yugoslavia, did you?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Those who killed these four were the army of Yugoslavia. You could see their green uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. You make that conclusion based upon the uniform they were wearing, don't you?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of the people who were killed there that day, you later learned that one of them was a KLA member who was then buried in the KLA cemetery, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: He was not buried in the KLA cemetery but in the cemetery of the civilians where the others were also buried. He was wearing no KLA uniform. He was dressed in civilian clothes. And he went to find a place to shelter his children.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But he was reburied in the KLA cemetery, wasn't he? This is Ramadan Xhokli.

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: He was reburied after three months after we returned from Italy. He was reburied by UNMIK, and he was reburied at the heroes' cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What you -- what you said in your statement, I just want to read the language and you tell me if this is true. "One of the 11 bodies which was initially buried in the cemetery, Ramadan Xhokli, was reburied in the KLA cemetery because he had been an active KLA member." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And to be eligible to be buried in a KLA cemetery, one had to be an active KLA member, didn't one?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: He was helping the KLA with foodstuffs. He was a member but responsible for providing foodstuffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was: To be eligible to be buried in a KLA cemetery, one had to be an active KLA member. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Maybe he was. I don't know. He's dead now. He's dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic. Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think we have any questions for this witness at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Just a couple questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, or good evening, sir, Mr. Lami. I'm Djuro Cepic, one of the Defence counsel on the Defence team of General Vladimir Lazarevic. You said that on the morning of the 13th of April the army came to your village and that is to say in the early morning hours. It was still dark, right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And it was a bit foggy, right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a bit foggy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But you could not see very well because it was early morning and it was still dark. You couldn't really see the faces of these persons who were entering the village, right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: People came by cars and went and hid in the mountains. At 5.00 in the morning, it was rather dark. But when the offensive started, it started at 6.30 and lasted until 8.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking you about the morning when they were coming before the offensive. You couldn't see them because it was early in the morning and it was still dark, right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No. We saw only the cars. We couldn't see the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You couldn't see any markings on those cars, right?

utterances.speaker: SEJDI LAMI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I haven't got any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cepic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would have some questions for this witness which are clarifications basically, but I have been informed that my exhibits are in the system. It won't take too long, 10 or 15 minutes, but I'm not sure they're in the system already, so it will be easier for us to deal with it tomorrow for 10 or 15 minutes. If it upsets your schedule in a serious way, I would be prepared to withdraw the questions I have, but I would need some additional clarification, so I would appreciate it if I could do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I didn't move my lips, Mr. Visnjic. Yeah, we'll do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lami, it's going to be necessary for you to come back tomorrow. We have to finish now for the evening. I don't think you'll be kept too long in the morning, but -- sorry, tomorrow afternoon. I'm sorry. You need to come back tomorrow afternoon when the evidence will begin at 2.15, but I don't think you'll be kept for long. Meanwhile, it's very important that between now and then you don't speak to anyone at all about your evidence, either the evidence you've given or the evidence that you may yet give here. Talk about anything else, but please keep off the subject of the evidence, and we shall see you again tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've noticed sometimes when I was not in the courtroom but watching the transcript that you have occasionally commented on the inefficiency of the cross-examinations and I just wanted to give you an opportunity to comment on the efficiency of the one that just took place, if you want to, but you don't need to if you don't want to, but I thought you might want that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm very grateful for what's happened today. In general, I think that I can detect a distinct effort being made to bring cross-examination within reasonable bounds. Obviously it's difficult to ensure that that's done completely, but I recognise the effort, and certainly in the case of this witness that was extremely efficient. But we are going to have to look more broadly at the whole way in which the case is proceeding. If may be necessary to have set aside time for a -- just a procedural hearing or a Status Conference probably before we have the break in October, so that when we come back if there are to be changes in the guidelines then they're in force by that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I really would like to emphasise something I said to you earlier because it's absolutely true from a lot of experience in my life. If you have prepared lawyers, they tend to move a lot more efficiently, and we have had recently had a lot more time to prepare because we've been working half days and we're starting communicate with each other better, and that's why you're seeing better cross-examinations, and that leads into a motion that I've filed today which you might want to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I knew there was bound to be an ulterior motive for you rising to your feet. I am not entirely convinced at the moment but remain to be persuaded about the merits of what you've just said and what's in your -- in your motion, but we shall debate that at a later stage, hopefully quite soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for keeping you further. Just one minute, please. I would like to add something to what Mr. Ackerman said. I would like to ask you kindly when you assess cross-examinations, would you please bear in mind a very special situation that we have to deal with in this case and that is the lack of documents and space and inaccessibility of both, our impossibility to reach documents that are in a sealed-off space for us. We cannot talk to people. If you look at other cases in this Tribunal that have to with Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, you have to bear in mind that Defence counsel in those cases can go to Zagreb, can have a look at documents, they can travel to Sarajevo and so on and so forth. We here have a special situation, whereas our possibilities are restricted in terms of investigation and exploring certain issues, and our cross-examination therefore suffers due to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may be an issue that has to be discussed a bit further, but now is not the moment for that. There will be an opportunity when we are looking at the programme ahead for you to raise issues of that nature. 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
